title: Diverticular disease and diverticulitis: symptoms, treatment and daily choices
intro: Diverticula are small pouches in the wall of the large bowel. Many people have them without symptoms, called diverticulosis. Diverticular disease describes symptoms or complications associated with them; diverticulitis means inflammation of the pouches. These terms do not all require the same treatment, and a previous diagnosis should not be used to explain every new abdominal symptom.

sections.heading: Distinguish a familiar pattern from a new acute illness
paragraphs: Intermittent lower abdominal discomfort, bloating, constipation or diarrhoea may occur with diverticular disease. Pain is often on the left, but its location alone does not establish the cause. Acute diverticulitis more often causes persistent local pain and tenderness, sometimes fever, nausea or altered stools. Similar symptoms can arise from other bowel, urinary or pelvic conditions. Explain when pain started, whether it is worsening, fever, bleeding, vomiting, passing stool or wind, medicines and previous episodes. Immune suppression and significant other illnesses can increase risk and may change how symptoms appear. Do not diagnose a recurrence solely because a scan once showed pouches.

sections.heading: Know when assessment is urgent
paragraphs: Worsening or persistent abdominal pain, fever or chills, blood in stool and inability to keep fluids down need prompt medical advice. Severe pain with a swollen abdomen, vomiting or inability to pass stool or wind may indicate obstruction or another complication and requires emergency assessment. Heavy rectal bleeding, fainting, confusion, marked breathlessness or signs of severe infection also need emergency help. Diverticular bleeding can occur without painful inflammation, but that does not make a large bleed safe. If you take anticoagulants or have reduced immunity, tell the team immediately. Do not wait for all warning signs to occur together or try to treat severe pain only with laxatives.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and treatment depend on severity
paragraphs: The clinician examines you and may request blood tests, stool tests or a CT scan to confirm the diagnosis, check complications and exclude other causes. A colonoscopy may be discussed after recovery, depending on findings, previous examination and persistent warning symptoms; it is not a routine self-arranged investigation during an acute painful attack. A person who is otherwise well with uncomplicated diverticulitis may be managed without antibiotics after clinical assessment and with clear follow-up. People who are unwell, immunosuppressed or have significant other illness are more likely to need antibiotics or hospital care. An abscess, perforation, obstruction or fistula may require drainage, surgery or other specialist treatment.

sections.heading: Plan eating, pain relief and recovery
paragraphs: During an acute episode, ask what you can eat and drink and when to increase intake; a clinician may advise a brief modified diet, but prolonged fasting or a long-term liquid diet is not a general solution. Seek reassessment if pain increases, fluids cannot be retained or improvement does not follow the agreed plan. Discuss suitable pain relief: paracetamol may be an option, while non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and opioid painkillers can be problematic and should not be started casually. Do not stop prescribed essential medicines without advice. Outside an acute episode, gradually increase dietary fibre if intake is low, with suitable fluids; individual fluid restrictions still apply. There is no general need to avoid nuts, seeds or fruit skins just because diverticula are present.

sections.heading: Review ongoing symptoms and surgery decisions
paragraphs: A balanced diet, activity as able and smoking cessation support general health, without guaranteeing that an attack cannot recur. A clinician may discuss constipation treatment or another explanation for persistent pain rather than repeated antibiotics. New weight loss, ongoing bleeding or a lasting change in bowel habit needs investigation, not automatic attribution to diverticula. Elective surgery is an individual decision based on complications, the burden of episodes, health, preferences and expected benefit rather than simply counting attacks. Ask about the chance of persistent symptoms, surgical complications, recovery and whether a stoma might be needed. Keep a plan for future flares and whom to contact out of hours.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: incidental pouches
examples.text: Ana's earlier examination found diverticula but she has no symptoms. She asks about balanced eating and appropriate fibre rather than starting antibiotics or removing every food containing seeds. If new persistent pain or bleeding appears, she will seek assessment rather than assume it is harmless.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: an acute change
examples.text: Milan has previously had intermittent discomfort, but now has constant worsening pain, fever and repeated vomiting. He seeks urgent assessment rather than taking a laxative and waiting for his next routine appointment. Severe pain with abdominal swelling or inability to pass wind would warrant emergency care.

questions: Do my symptoms represent uncomplicated inflammation, a complication or another condition?
What is my treatment, food and fluid plan, and when should improvement or review occur?
Do I need further bowel investigation or a personalised discussion about surgery after recovery?
